title: Computational_heuristic_intelligence
summary:
Computational heuristic intelligence (CHI) refers to specialized programming techniques in computational intelligence (also called artificial intelligence) that have the express goal of avoiding complexity issues, also called NP-hard problems, by using human-like techniques.

The legal systems of all modern human societies employ both heuristics (generalizations of cases) from individual trial records as well as legislated statutes (rules) as regulatory guides, providing an analogy for how CHI approaches problem-solving.

Another approach to the avoidance of complexity issues is to employ feedback control rather than feedforward modeling as a problem-solving paradigm. This approach has been called computational cybernetics, because the term "computational" is associated with conventional computer programming techniques which represent a strategic, compiled, or feedforward model of the problem, and the term "cybernetic" is associated with conventional system operation techniques which represent a tactical, interpreted, or feedback model of the problem.

Research by Dyer (2012) and Feldman (2004) independently investigated somatic governance paradigms, specifically control of a simple jointed limb by a single flexor muscle. They found that it is impossible to determine forces from limb positions, meaning the problem cannot have a pre-computed (feedforward) mathematical solution. Global postures and limb positions are commanded in feedforward terms using global displacements (common coding), with the forces needed being computed locally by feedback loops. CHI falls under the broader umbrella of computational intelligence, which traditionally rests on three main pillars: Neural Networks, Fuzzy Systems, and Evolutionary Computation.
